# Embeddings and Representation Learning {#sec-embeddings}

The retrieval of @sec-rag-retrieval leaned on a model that maps a query and a
chunk into one vector space, a dual-encoder, with a cross-encoder reranker and
ColBERT's late interaction as the more expressive cousins. That chapter used
those models. It did not say how they come to place related text near each other.
This chapter does. By the end a reader can explain why an embedding model is
trained against a contrastive objective rather than next-token prediction, why
the choice of negatives is the central design variable, how one model serves many
tasks and many vector sizes, and how the strongest 2025 embedders are
bootstrapped from large language models.

## A geometry you can compare

A language model is trained to predict the next token, and nothing in that
objective asks two texts that mean the same thing to land near each other. Its
hidden states carry meaning, but the space is not metric: cosine distance in it
does not track relatedness, so pooling a decoder's states gives a mediocre
retriever. Retrieval needs the opposite of generation. It needs a space where a
single distance, computed once and indexed, ranks a million chunks against a
query. The embedding model exists to learn that space, and it is trained for it
directly rather than borrowed from a generator.

## The contrastive objective

The principle is to pull a positive pair together and push negatives apart.
InfoNCE, introduced for contrastive predictive coding [@oord2018cpc], scores a
query $q$ against its positive $d^{+}$ and a set of negatives $\{d^{-}_j\}$ as a
softmax over similarities, with a temperature $\tau$:

$$
\mathcal{L} = -\log
\frac{\exp(\operatorname{sim}(q, d^{+})/\tau)}
{\exp(\operatorname{sim}(q, d^{+})/\tau) + \sum_j \exp(\operatorname{sim}(q, d^{-}_j)/\tau)}
$$

The model learns by discrimination, not reconstruction: it never has to generate
the document, only to rank the right one above the wrong ones. Sentence-BERT made
this practical for whole sentences with a siamese dual-encoder whose outputs
compare by cosine [@reimers2019sbert], against the alternative of a BERT
cross-encoder that is accurate but must run on every pair and so cannot scan a
corpus (the same bi-encoder-versus-cross-encoder split @sec-rag-retrieval draws
at retrieval time, here decided at training time).

## Negatives are the design variable

The positive is given; the skill is in what you push away. Drawing negatives at
random teaches only coarse distinctions, so two moves dominate the recipes. The
first is in-batch negatives: Dense Passage Retrieval treats the other positives
in a training batch as negatives for each query, so a larger batch buys more
negatives almost for free and a bigger batch directly raises retrieval quality
[@karpukhin2020dense]. The second is hard negatives, wrong-but-plausible passages
that force a finer boundary, usually mined with a cheap lexical retriever.
RocketQA sharpens both, adding cross-batch negatives and denoising the hard
negatives, because a passage retrieved as a negative is sometimes actually
relevant, a false negative that punishes the model for being right
[@qu2021rocketqa].

When labeled pairs are scarce, augmentation manufactures a positive. SimCSE makes
its positive pair by encoding the same sentence twice under different dropout
masks, an almost-free perturbation that works surprisingly well, and its
supervised form draws positives from natural-language-inference entailment pairs
[@gao2021simcse].

Average the loss over many queries as the negatives are drawn closer to the
query, and watch it climb.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = 32

def infonce(q, dpos, dnegs, tau=0.05):
    sims = np.array([q @ dpos] + [q @ x for x in dnegs]) / tau
    sims -= sims.max()                        # numerical stability
    p = np.exp(sims) / np.exp(sims).sum()
    return -np.log(p[0])                       # loss = -log P(positive)

def unit(v): return v / np.linalg.norm(v)

def mean_loss(hardness, n, trials=300):        # hardness 0=random, ->1 toward query
    total = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        q = unit(rng.normal(size=d))
        dpos = unit(q + 0.4 * rng.normal(size=d))
        negs = [unit(hardness * q + (1 - hardness) * rng.normal(size=d)) for _ in range(n)]
        total += infonce(q, dpos, negs)
    return total / trials

for h in [0.0, 0.3, 0.6]:
    print(f"negative hardness {h:.1f}: mean loss = {mean_loss(h, 16):.3f}")
print("harder negatives (closer to the query) -> larger loss -> stronger signal")
```
::::

## One model, many tasks and many sizes

A single embedder is asked to serve search, clustering, classification, and
deduplication at once, and two ideas stretch one model across that range. The
first conditions the embedding on a task instruction: Instructor prepends a short
description of the task so the same weights produce a query embedding tuned for
retrieval or for similarity without per-task fine-tuning [@su2022instructor]. The
second makes the vector size itself a dial. Matryoshka representation learning
trains so that the first $m$ dimensions of the embedding are themselves a usable
embedding, as accurate as one trained natively at $m$, at no additional training
cost [@kusupati2022matryoshka]. You store the full vector once and truncate it
per query, trading accuracy for index cost without retraining.

## Where the training pairs come from

The bottleneck is rarely the loss; it is the supply of query-document pairs. The
weakly-supervised route mines them at scale: E5 pretrains contrastively on
hundreds of millions of naturally occurring pairs, posts and comments, titles and
bodies, before a small supervised fine-tune [@wang2022e5]. The route that now
leads instead bootstraps from a generator. E5-mistral prompts a large language
model to synthesize diverse retrieval tasks and their query-document pairs, then
fine-tunes Mistral-7B itself into the embedder, reaching the top of the
benchmarks with little human-labeled data [@wang2023e5mistral]. The generative
model trains the retrieval model, a clean instance of the synthetic-data loop of
@sec-synthetic-data. A third route distills the cross-encoder of
@sec-rag-retrieval into a bi-encoder, transferring the accuracy of full
query-document interaction into the cost of a single dot product.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether one general embedder can dominate is unsettled. MTEB, which scores
embedders across classification, clustering, retrieval, reranking, and semantic
similarity, found that no single model wins every task, so a leaderboard number
hides which task it was won on [@muennighoff2022mteb]. One camp reads this as
temporary, a stronger LLM-bootstrapped embedder will generalize across all of
them; the other reads it as structural, because the geometry that separates
topics for clustering is not the geometry that ranks answers for retrieval, which
is exactly why instruction-conditioning exists. Treat an embedding leaderboard
score as task-shaped until tested on your own retrieval distribution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The vector index reaches back into how the representation is trained. The serving
cost of retrieval scales with the embedding dimension times the corpus size
(@sec-rag-retrieval), and that cost, paid on every query forever, is what
justifies training for truncatability in the first place: Matryoshka exists
because a 1024-dimensional vector over a billion chunks is expensive enough that
being able to drop to 256 dimensions without retraining is worth designing for.
The retrieval layer's cost dictates the shape of the vector the training run is
asked to produce.
:::
